content: The studies described focus on various interventions aimed at improving HIV prevention, testing, treatment adherence, and care engagement among key populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender individuals, and people living with HIV (PLHIV) in different settings. Below is a professional summary of the findings and methodologies: 1. Study on Mobile App for HIV Testing Among MSM in the USA: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving 113 HIV-negative MSM compared the use of a mobile app (Status Update Project) that provided HIV testing reminders, prevention information, and STI education to a monthly health survey or no intervention. The study faced a high risk of bias due to inadequate documentation of randomization and allocation processes, baseline differences between groups, and self-reported outcomes without laboratory validation. By the 8-month follow-up, the intervention group had a 21% loss to follow-up compared to 12% in the control group. Blinding was not feasible, and deviations from the intervention were not documented. 2. Cohort Study on Web-Based HIV/STI Testing for PLHIV Soon to Be Released from Prison: This study included 238 HIV-positive adults nearing release from prison. It compared a personalized online HIV/STI testing website to a standard online provider directory. The study did not adjust for baseline and time-varying confounders, and the intervention group consisted of those who received a case management video conference before release. The control group included those who did not receive the intervention in time. The study was assessed for bias using the ROBINS-I tool. 3. Digital HIV Care Navigation for Young MSM and Transgender Women: A cohort study among 120 HIV-positive individuals aged 18–34 compared those who completed a 6-month digital HIV care navigation program (text messaging with a personal HIV care navigator) to those who did not complete the intervention. Half of the participants were lost to follow-up, with reasons including phone loss, relocation, or unknown causes. The intervention group consisted of those who completed the program, while the control group included those who did not. The study faced challenges with blinding and self-reported outcomes, and the small sample size contributed to imprecision. 4. Mobile App Intervention for ART Adherence Among Stimulant-Using MSM: An RCT involving 90 HIV-positive stimulant-using MSM in the USA compared a mobile app (APP+) with HIV/ART content, interactive storytelling, and medication self-monitoring to no intervention. Blinding was not possible, and self-reported outcomes introduced potential detection bias. 5. CARE+ Corrections Intervention for PLHIV Released from Prison: This RCT among 110 HIV-positive adults compared a computerized motivational interview and risk reduction plan (CARE+ Corrections) with text messaging for care navigation post-release to an attention-control intervention (opioid overdose prevention video and HIV provider resources). Adjustments were made for study location, gender, sexual orientation, depressive symptoms, and PTSD scores. 6. Telemedicine for HIV Care in Prisoners: A cohort study among 1,201 HIV-positive prisoners in the USA compared telemedicine-based HIV care to standard on-site management by correctional facility physicians. The control group consisted of individuals receiving care before telemedicine implementation. The study was assessed for bias using ROBINS-I and was downgraded for moderate concerns in one domain. Baseline and time-varying confounders were not adjusted. 7. Social Media Campaign for Syphilis Testing in MSM: A cross-sectional study in Canada evaluated the impact of a social media campaign targeting MSM during a syphilis outbreak. Ads on platforms like Grindr and Facebook directed users to an informational website. The study used multivariable Poisson regression to calculate the rate ratio of syphilis testing frequency before and after the campaign. However, the intervention was not considered targeted health information as it lacked personalization beyond geotagging and platform-specific targeting. 8. Peer Navigation for HIV Care Engagement: Peer navigation interventions were reviewed for their effectiveness in improving linkage to care, treatment initiation, and retention among key populations. While peer navigation has shown promise in some settings, its effectiveness has not been consistently demonstrated across all outcomes. The WHO has recommended peer support and navigation approaches for linkage to care following an HIV diagnosis but lacks specific recommendations for key populations. 9. Systematic Review of Peer Navigation Interventions: A systematic review identified four studies on the effectiveness of peer navigation for HIV care, two on values and preferences, and none on costs. The studies included RCTs and observational designs, focusing on populations such as prisoners, transgender individuals, and sex workers. Peer navigation was often part of multi-component interventions, including community empowerment and contingency management. Overall, these studies highlight the potential of digital and peer-based interventions to improve HIV-related outcomes but also underscore the challenges of bias, small sample sizes, and reliance on self-reported data. Further research is needed to establish the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of these approaches in diverse populations and settings.
